# Šw: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Šw** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**Born from Atum.** In the oldest Egyptian creation account we possess — Pyramid Text Utterance 600, inscribed in the royal pyramids of the late Old Kingdom — the creator Atum stands alone on the primeval hill in the waters of Nun and, without companion, brings forth the first two gods: he sneezes Shu and spits Tefnut, the sacred text says, and the wordplay is the theology.  Shu's very name (šw) echoes the sneeze, Tefnut's the spittle; the world begins with the creator's own body discharging itself into differentiation.  The Coffin Texts (spells 75–80) expand the scene: Atum, alone in Nun, says he was not built by any builder, and then — 'I sneezed Shu, I spat Tefnut'.

**Shu Lifts the Sky.** Shu and Tefnut beget the twins Geb (earth) and Nut (sky), but the children are locked in an embrace that leaves no room for life.  Shu places himself in the interval and raises Nut above his head, arching her body into the starry vault — the posture the Egyptians gave him forever: kneeling or standing, arms lifted, the cosmic pillar.  The image saturates Egyptian religion.

**Shu and Tefnut in Nubia.** A late myth tells how Tefnut quarrelled with Shu and departed south to Nubia, taking the form of a lioness — or, in the Demotic telling, of a cat travelling with her companion baboon.  The land dried behind her; the south wind brought no relief.  Shu sent Thoth, master of words, disguised as a baboon, to talk her home; his flood of eloquence — stories, flattery, argument, and embedded animal fables — accomplished what force could not.

## The Name Travels

The Greeks associated Shu with Atlas, the Titan who holds up the celestial sphere — a comparison of function, not of name, since no Greek rendering of šw is attested; modern scholars repeat the comparison on the same grounds.  In Egyptian theology Shu could merge with Re (as the rays of sunlight) and with Onuris, the warrior god.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Šw** stands at [/shu/](/shu/) — [lore](/shu/lore/), [scholars](/shu/scholars/), [patterns](/shu/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can express — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it, mechanically, in Tier-1.
